title: Laws, Fate, and the Seventh Day
english: It has been completed, rather than being filled; it lies there. For it is not their existence that has been completed, but their making, just as we say also concerning the poetic arts, which bring the end through their activities, saying that the ship or the house has been completed.

Thus the heaven has been completed, having received its proper harmony, which received its fullness from both the firmament and the luminaries and also from the stars, and the earth from both the animals and the various plants. And when each of them had become, the 'has been completed' did not fit; but now, having received the concord and the harmony of all things, the 'The heaven and the earth and all their world were completed' follows.

And it is said that the world of the earth and its fullness according to what is said: 'The earth is the Lord's and its fullness' (Ps 24:1). Because even the variety of the heaven is called a world, Moses himself says concerning them in his words: 'Not looking up to the heaven and seeing the sun and the moon and the stars, all the world of the heaven, being led astray, you shall worship them' (Deut 4:19), who through the position which was set by God, demonstrate beauty, some by moving in these circulations, others to be with these, some making their motion in a straight line, and others in an arc.

An army of heaven, therefore, because of the arrangement, has been said according to what has been said: 'Whose hands made all the host of heaven' (Job 38:7). Concerning which, those who have not understood well have erred, introducing fate and setting all things by necessity, defining the stars to be determining the poetic lives of men and the things happening to others, who, for a sign, if not for the doing, have been set according to also... concerning those having happened on the fourth day, we demonstrated the 'Let them be for signs and for seasons and for months and for years' (Gen 1:14), setting forth as if human life has not been compelled by the stars. For those escaping life through war and universal accidents are not under one formation. And moreover, the argument of fate is more strongly overturned.

From the laws: all Jews, having reached the eighth day from birth, are circumcised, and they receive the trial of iron even from the sprouts [infants], and no one could say how all at once they cast [the foreskin] off within a single hour, almost everywhere on earth and every day as Jews are born; but they say that even certain Ethiopians have the membranes of the genitals removed at the same time as birth, and even these do not all have their birth at once; and altogether the various customs and laws according to the nations negate fate. If this does not fit according to fate, much more do the things of choice. For if fate leads the happening by necessity, and choice has power over the possible things, fate will not be about these things. For virtue and vice have benefited or harmed the one possessing them, and each of those doing [actions] is blamed because of the bad habits, or praised for acting rightly; but the things happening by necessity [omitted]... no one accepts or blames the one doing something by necessity. Furthermore, if the laws are from fate, and those not obeying these are not from fate, it seems to negate and overturn fate itself. Significant, then, are the stars, not as makers, but signifying the weather or pestilential occurrences or something else that seems to the one foreseeing, and these things are about this.

Let us return to the thing set forth from the beginning: 'And God finished on the sixth day his works, which he made' (Gen 2:2), which indicates as if the completion is about the only ones which he has made. For there are works which have not yet happened, which were foretold as being to come, such as the resurrection of the dead and entirely those things which are to be according to providence, which happen in their own sequence from God. So the addition 'of the works which he made' is appropriately placed. It is also necessary to contemplate this, that God did not 'rest' (Gen 2:2) in the seventh without having acted, for already all things were completed; but he 'blessed' (Gen 2:3) only the seventh day and sanctified it, and the saying leads to this: 'That in it he rested from all his works, which God began to make' (Gen 2:2). 'Which he began'—for it is not the beginning of all the works...
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: Perception and Deception
english: During one of the six days, angels and archangels and all the spiritual essence did not receive a beginning. And because this is so, God himself says in Job: 'When the stars were created, all my angels shouted to me with a great voice' (Job 38:7). Therefore, having been created. Because of this, the saying is confirmed, saying: 'If the spirit of the ruler rises upon you, do not leave your place' (Luke 10:19). For this pretext becomes the cause of many evils, with the devil having cast down something even greater, which now works by introducing a slander against God, as if because of the command not to take hold of only the known good and evil, but also to prevent them from becoming gods, as if he saw them about to become gods.

Indeed, from this deception, the whole heresy called Ophite was established, which exalts the serpent greatly concerning him, as they think, saying: in whom, they say, God intended man to be in wickedness, calling wickedness to be the not-knowing of good and evil; thus they say this craftily: He, they say, made man in good things; and they mythologize other things about the serpent, slandering him whom they have raised up as a god to themselves. However, the serpent performs his deception well, persuading them only to have an opening not for good, just as the apostle said: 'I wish you to be wise unto good, blameless unto evil' (Romans 16:19).

But the serpent, wanting them to be wise unto evil, wished to open those eyes running toward this, who, while virtue is at work, are not opened but happen to be closed, remaining blind, which Jesus says he works in the Gospel, saying: 'I came that those who do not see might see, and those who see might become blind' (John 9:39). But Jesus, according to history, has made no one blind, but has granted sight to the blind. It is therefore evident that he makes those who see badly blind, and makes those who are useful to see again with the useful eyes, who, being the inner man, saving the ability to see clearly not sensually but intellectually, before knowing and imposing reason upon the sense, they hide...

Regarding what was said in the 82nd [section]: 'The wise will hide perception.' And so that what is said may become clear through an example: perception is the tactile sense of hot and cold, hard and soft, rough and smooth; and to the irrational and the child, these things are manifest through touch. But when the physician comes to feel the pulse, he hides the perception, providing a reason through the movement of the throbbing vessels. In the same way, the laypeople perceive images by sense alone, but the scribes contemplate them with the logic of the eye.

Thus the man, before the transgression, was looking at things with a mind that was scientifically applying understanding to things, as is necessary. As long as he had these eyes directing themselves toward appropriate spectacles, he did not know evil; instead of testing it, he did not accept it. But when these eyes grew dim, and those leaning toward evil were opened, then he also became cast out.

The devil, having this will, seeks to make the woman wise, introducing envy to conceive of God, and promising great things, so that by these things he might entice, saying: 'You shall become like gods, knowing good and evil' (Gen 3:5), while also subverting her intention with more views, lest the idolatry through images be joined, all while flattering the angels who are with him.

3, 6–7. And she saw that the tree was good for food and that it was pleasing to the eyes and beautiful for understanding, and having taken of its fruit she ate, and she gave also to her husband with her, and they ate, and the eyes of the two were opened and they knew that they were naked. Holding fast to the deception of the serpent, she made for him a trial that was the opposite of it; for that which lies out for food is not tested by sight, except that once the deception has begun, it works a certain pleasure and enjoyment, even if it thus rouses the deceived to action.

After having perceived according to the deceptions of the serpent spoken of, she took it through consent and ate, performing the act of a finished work, and she receives the man as a partner, doing and distributing the things toward deception; for such is perception, of which we thought the woman possessed a reason.
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Deception of the Senses
english: Once the eyes were opened, they knew that they were naked (Gen 2:25). For this happens to those being deceived. For after the activity of their wickedness is made manifest, they come to realize that they were stripped of virtue; this is granted again by the pitiless God, so that he who works wickedness might not remain entirely insensate and stay completely outside of virtue.

This is the deception of the devil: that he makes the things seen according to the true logic by the eye of the pure soul to be seen conversely, supposing the pleasant instead of the good, and showing the good as something harmful. Thus also eyes are opened which previously were usefully closed. For there is in the soul an eye which imposes itself upon the intelligible through itself, but there is that which follows from instruction by another, which the serpent having perverted, filled the things of deception, so that both sensation and the mind would undergo harm; for when sensation suffers perversion, then also the opinions of the mind become diverted.

It has been said concerning those who have used things contrary: 'Woe to those saying the evil is good and the good is evil' (1 Tim 5:22). Thus, pleasures were raised up as the cause of errors; for even those in wisdom say they prefer the pleasant. For many prefer the easy way over virtue, not accepting the strenuous, and they are stripped because of it. Therefore, the pleasant things must be despised, since they become a hypothesis for sins.

There are some who say that 'Adam ate with it' (Gen 3:6) indicates his consent, so that he might not be utterly destroyed, agreeing with what was said by Paul: 'Adam was not deceived, but the woman, having been deceived, came into transgression' (1 Tim 2:14), as if he were able to turn away from the wickedness through her also. And they sewed fig leaves and made themselves girdles. And they heard the voice of the Lord walking in the garden, the cowardly ones, and both Adam and his wife fled from the face of God amidst the tree of the paradise (Gen 3:8). Remaining with the things previously viewed concerning the paradise and Adam and the woman, we connect these things. Since they knew that they were naked...
